explanation: OEIS A105751: '(ii) for the other primes of type 2, the p-adic valuation v_p(a(n)) ~ n/(p − 1)', where type-2 primes are conjectured to be p ≡ 1 (mod 4) together with 2. The formal statement takes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) prime and asserts (p − 1) v_p(a(n))/n → 1, combining the conjectured identification of type-2 primes with the asymptotic, which is how the comment's conjecture reads. Faithful.

Compared against OEIS A105751 (imaginary part of Π_{k=0..n} (1 + k i)), comments by P. Bala (2023): 'We conjecture that the set of type 2 primes consists of primes p == 1 (mod 4) [...] together with the prime p = 2' and 'Moll's conjecture 5.5 extends to this sequence and takes the form: (i) the 2-adic valuation v_2(a(n)) ~ n/4 as n -> oo. (ii) for the other primes of type 2, the p-adic valuation v_p(a(n)) ~ n/(p - 1) as n -> oo.' The Lean statement is (ii) for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4): (p − 1)·v_p(a(n))/n → 1 in ℚ. It therefore combines (ii) with the conjectured description of the type 2 primes, as its docstring says. a takes Int.floor of the imaginary part, which is exact because the product is a Gaussian integer (tests: 0, 1, 3, 0, −40). padicValInt p 0 = 0 would spoil the limit if a(n) vanished infinitely often, but a(n) = 0 only at n = 0 and n = 3 for n ≤ 3000 (computed), and a zero forces Π_{k≤n}(1 + k²) to be a perfect square. Numerically (p − 1)·v_p(a(3000))/3000 = 1.000, 1.000, 0.997, 0.989 for p = 5, 13, 17, 29. Correct.
